mcqs.question: In a 5-node cluster requiring a majority quorum, how many node failures can the cluster tolerate while still making progress, and why?
options: 2 failures — a majority of 5 is 3, and the remaining 3 nodes can still form a majority on their own
4 failures — as long as 1 node survives, it can act alone
0 failures — all 5 nodes must always be reachable
1 failure — losing more than one node breaks the quorum inequality entirely
mcqs.explanation: A majority of 5 nodes is 3, so the cluster keeps working as long as any 3 of the 5 remain reachable — meaning it tolerates 2 failures. A single surviving node cannot form a majority alone, and the cluster doesn't need all 5 nodes up to make progress.

mcqs.question: In Raft, a leader appends a log entry and then crashes before any follower replicates it. What happens to that entry?
options: It stays committed because the leader itself wrote it durably
It is not considered committed, since a majority never durably stored it, and can be safely discarded by whichever node becomes the next leader
The cluster becomes permanently stuck and cannot elect a new leader
It is automatically committed once any single follower catches up, regardless of majority
mcqs.explanation: Raft only considers an entry committed once a majority of nodes have durably stored it — the leader's own copy alone isn't enough. Since no follower got it before the crash, it's safely discardable, and this doesn't block a new election, which only requires a majority vote on leadership, not on every uncommitted entry.

mcqs.question: In two-phase commit, why can't a participant that voted "yes" during the prepare phase simply abort on its own if it doesn't hear back from the coordinator?
options: Participants are technically allowed to abort unilaterally at any time after voting yes
Because voting yes obligates the participant to commit if told to, and unilaterally aborting could conflict with other participants that were told to commit, breaking atomicity
Because the prepare phase doesn't actually require participants to lock any resources
Because two-phase commit doesn't have a concept of voting at all
mcqs.explanation: Once a participant votes yes, it has committed to following the coordinator's eventual instruction — it can't know whether other participants were told to commit, so backing out alone risks the whole transaction becoming inconsistent. This locking-in is exactly why coordinator failure causes blocking; participants do lock resources during prepare, and voting is central to the protocol.

mcqs.question: A team is building a checkout flow spanning an orders service, a payments service, and an inventory service, and wants high availability even if one service is temporarily slow. Which pattern fits better, and why?
options: Two-phase commit, because it's the only pattern that provides real atomicity
Neither pattern is appropriate for cross-service transactions
Two-phase commit, because sagas cannot handle more than two participants
A saga, because it avoids holding cross-service locks and keeps each service available even if another step is temporarily slow, at the cost of needing compensating actions
mcqs.explanation: A saga's defining trade-off — no cross-service lock held, each step commits independently — is exactly what preserves availability when one service is slow; 2PC would instead hold locks across all three services waiting on the coordinator. Sagas handle any number of participants, and 2PC's atomicity comes at a real availability cost this scenario cares about.

mcqs.question: A 2PC coordinator crashes after all participants voted yes but before sending the final commit decision. What is the immediate consequence for those participants?
options: They remain blocked, holding their locks, unable to safely commit or abort on their own until the coordinator recovers or a recovery mechanism intervenes
They automatically abort after a short timeout with no other effect
They automatically commit since they already voted yes
They immediately elect a new coordinator among themselves and proceed
mcqs.explanation: This is 2PC's defining flaw: a participant that voted yes cannot unilaterally decide to commit or abort, because it doesn't know what other participants were told — it must wait, holding its locks, for the coordinator to recover or for an external recovery process. Plain 2PC has no built-in coordinator re-election or safe auto-decision.

mcqs.question: A service writes an order to its own database and needs to reliably notify a shipping service, without using a distributed transaction across the two services. Which pattern addresses this?
options: Two-phase commit run without a coordinator
The outbox pattern — write the state change and an "event to publish" in the same local transaction, then a separate process reliably delivers the event
A saga with no compensating transactions defined
Simply calling the shipping service's API directly inside the same local database transaction
mcqs.explanation: The outbox pattern gets atomicity for the local write and the outgoing event by keeping both in one local transaction, then relies on a separate reliable publisher for cross-service delivery — avoiding a distributed transaction entirely. 2PC needs a coordinator by definition, a saga without compensations isn't safe, and calling another service's API inside a local DB transaction doesn't make that call transactional.
